q: Which of the following is a composite slab?
n: Figure B, concrete cast on a profiled steel deck that acts with it, is a composite slab. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 5 (composite members); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which of the following is a post-tensioned slab?
n: Figure E shows draped tendons tensioned after casting: a post-tensioned slab. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 4 (prestressed concrete); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which of the following is a precast slab?
n: Figure D shows precast units seated on supports: a precast slab. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which of the following is a one-way ribbed slab?
n: Figure A has closely spaced ribs spanning one way: a one-way ribbed (joist) slab. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; NSCP 2015 Chapter 4.

q: Which of the following represents a one-way slab and beam system?
n: Figure C, a slab carried on parallel beams that bends in one direction, is a one-way slab and beam system. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; NSCP 2015 Chapter 4.

q: Identify item A, which distributes loads and provides compressive strength.
n: Item A is the concrete slab, which distributes loads and provides the compressive strength of the composite deck. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 5 (composite design); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Identify item B, which serves as a permanent formwork and contributes to slab strength.
n: Item B is the profiled steel sheeting (metal deck). It is permanent formwork and acts as tension reinforcement with the concrete. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 5; Steel Deck Institute.

q: Identify item C, which acts as the main support for the composite deck.
n: Item C is the steel beam's top flange, the main support for the composite deck. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 5.

q: Identify item D, which locks the concrete slab and beam together to resist shear forces.
n: Item D is the shear connectors (headed studs) welded to the beam. They lock slab and beam together to transfer horizontal shear. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 5 (Sec. 5I, composite members).

q: Identify item E, which provides tensile strength at the top layer of the slab.
n: Item E is the top steel reinforcement (mesh), which gives tensile strength at the top of the slab and controls cracking. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 4.

q: What type of slab system is shown in Figure A?
n: Figure A has ribs running one way between voids: a ribbed (one-way joist) slab. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What type of slab is shown in Figure B?
n: Figure B is a slab framed by beams on all four sides: a two-way slab and beam system. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; NSCP 2015 Chapter 4.

q: What type of slab is shown in Figure C?
n: Figure C is a flat plate: a uniform slab on columns with no beams, drop panels or capitals. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What type of slab does Figure D refer to?
n: Figure D projects past its single support: a cantilevered slab. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Where is the device in Figure E typically used?
n: Figure E is a tendon anchorage, used in post-tensioned concrete structures. Source: Post-Tensioning Institute; NSCP 2015 Chapter 4 (prestressed concrete).

q: What is the area of a trapezoidal pavement with parallel sides of 15 m and 10 m and a depth of 8 m?
n: Area of a trapezoid = (a + b) ÷ 2 × h = (15 + 10) ÷ 2 × 8 = 100 m². Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (area computation).

q: That trapezoidal pavement is 4 in. thick. What is its volume?
n: Volume = 100 m² × 4 in (0.1016 m) ≈ 10.2 m³, or about 10 m³. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: A concrete pavement is 4.00 m wide, 22.0 m long and 125 mm thick. How many 40 kg bags of cement does a Class C mix need?
n: Volume = 4.00 × 22.0 × 0.125 = 11.0 m³. A Class C mix (1:3:6) uses 6.0 bags of 40 kg cement per m³, so 11.0 × 6.0 = 66 bags. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 1-2.

q: For the same 11.0 m³ Class C pavement (0.50 m³ of sand per m³), how many cubic meters of sand are needed, rounded up?
n: Class C needs 0.50 m³ of sand per m³: 11.0 × 0.50 = 5.5 m³, ordered as 6 m³. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 1-2.

q: For the same 11.0 m³ Class C pavement (1.0 m³ of gravel per m³), how many cubic meters of gravel are needed?
n: Class C needs 1.0 m³ of gravel per m³: 11.0 × 1.0 = 11 m³. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 1-2.

q: What concrete mix is standard for slabs and beams?
n: Class A concrete (1:2:4) is the standard mix for slabs, beams, columns and other structural members. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate; DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405.

q: What is the typical strength of concrete for slabs and beams?
n: Slabs and beams typically use about 3,000 psi (≈21 MPa) concrete, the common minimum f'c for structural members. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 419; DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405.

q: What is the maximum allowable slump for concrete used in beams and slabs (in millimeters)?
n: Concrete for beams and slabs is usually limited to about 100 mm slump for workability without segregation. Source: DPWH Standard Specifications, Item 405; ACI 211.1.

q: What is the minimum concrete cover required for a slab on fill?
n: Concrete cast against and permanently exposed to earth needs 75 mm cover. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 420.6.1 (Table 420.6.1.3.1).

q: Without computing deflection, what is the minimum thickness of a simply supported one-way slab?
n: Without deflection checks, a simply supported one-way solid slab must be at least L/20 thick. Source: NSCP 2015, Table 407.3.1.1.

q: What is the thickened or deepened part of a beam that develops greater moment resistance near supports?
n: A haunch is a thickened or deepened part of a beam near its supports that increases moment and shear resistance. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: If a beam stays within its elastic limit, what happens when the load is removed?
o: It returns to its original shape
It keeps deforming under slight load
n: Within its elastic limit a beam behaves elastically and returns to its original shape when the load is removed. Source: Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials.

q: What deformation is typical in a loaded beam?
n: Deflection, the vertical displacement under load, is the typical deformation of a loaded beam. Source: Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials.

q: If a beam pour can't be finished in one go, where should it stop?
n: Construction joints in beams go near midspan (middle third), where shear is lowest. Source: ACI 301; NSCP 2015, Sec. 426.5.6.

q: Besides resisting shear, what do stirrups do in a beam?
o: Hold the longitudinal bars in place
n: Besides resisting shear, stirrups hold the longitudinal bars in position, forming the reinforcing cage. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 425.7; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is a perimeter beam called?
n: A spandrel beam is a perimeter beam along the edge of a floor or roof. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What members support floors?
n: Joists are closely spaced members that support floors. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What carries smaller beams?
n: Girders are large beams that carry smaller beams. A girder spans between columns and receives the reactions of the beams framing into it. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is an additional structural element placed to support structures above?
n: A corbel is a bracket projecting from a wall or column to support a member above. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; NSCP 2015, Sec. 416.5 (brackets and corbels).
